speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-98, to establish the office of parliamentary commissioner.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH OFFICE OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH OFFICE OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill provides authority for the appointment of a parliamentary commissioner whose duty it shall be to investigate any grievance protesting administrative decisions of government departments and/or crown companies which may be registered by a petitioner. The commissioner, however, shall not investigate any decision with respect to which there is a right of appeal to a court or tribunal, and at his discretion may refuse to investigate those grievances which are either trivial or which he considers have not been placed before him in good faith.
The bill also provides that if no action is taken by the administrative head of a department following the recommendations of the commissioner, the commissioner may then at his discretion send a copy of his report and recommendation to the Prime Minister and may thereafter make such reports to parliament as he sees fit, designed to curb any possible abuse of administrative power. This legislation is similar to legislation enacted in several other countries.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

The purpose of this bill is to restore, in so far as the parliament of Canada is legislatively able, Remembrance day to the position intended within the spirit and meaning of the Remembrance Day Act, revised statutes, chapter 237. Throughout Canada in each and every year, the 11th day of November, being the day in the year 1918 on which the great war was triumphantly concluded by an armistice, shall be a holiday, and shall be kept and observed as such under the name of Remembrance day.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for giving notice of his intention to ask this question. This possibility, therefore, is not presently under consideration.

speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton South. In the interests of the accuracy of the record and for our own benefit, perhaps the hon. member might defer his remarks for 15 to 20 seconds in order to let those members leave who may wish to do so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take very much of the time of the house this afternoon on second reading of the bill. Rather, I am inclined to accept the suggestion made by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate yesterday when he called for a shortening of the debate on second reading in the hope that we can move this 27507-3-151J
Atlantic Development Board measure into a committee of the house, perhaps the committee on banking and commerce, and deal with it more fully at that particular stage.
I think it is quite apparent that we in this group have approached this measure on a non-partisan basis. We have suggested there was hope that this type of measure might make some substantial and concrete contribution to the curing of the economic ills of the Atlantic region of Canada. We tried to be objective. We pointed out that we were concerned about certain aspects of this legislation as it came forward. We indicated certain fears and certain reservations that we held. At the same time we attempted to fulfil our responsibility as members of the opposition, and we brought forward proposals that I think were to some extent constructive and objective, but apparently to no avail.
I suggest it is not an exaggeration to say, bearing in mind the statements that have been made in this house by members of the government and attempting to relate the legislation before us to the Atlantic provinces, that this bill represents nothing more than a straw in the wind, a leaf on the tidal waters, a measure that is going to be completely inadequate in attempting to cope with the situation in the Atlantic provinces. I suggest that this is a form of political subterfuge. It is a concession to expedience at its worst.
In this connection I should like to indicate that I am amazed at the public statements that have been made by some of the official representatives of the Atlantic provinces economic council now that the bill is before us in all its inadequacy and all its shortcomings. It seems to me it is quite regrettable that in the concern of this organization, APEC, to remain politically non-partisan and in their anxiety and keen desire to obtain at least some concrete reaction from this government to our proposals, they are prepared so passively and so meekly to accept this token recognition of our problems. I sincerely trust that in their later, more formal and more official pronouncements on the specific bill, which they can now study "in all of its detail, they will be less concerned about offending the government and more concerned about pressing for a truly effective board capable of initiating decisive action.
There are many aspects of the bill regarding which we intend to introduce specific amendments at the appropriate time, and I hope the minister and the government will give them due consideration. In its present form and under the proposed terms of reference that are before us, I suggest that the bill is a miserable piece of legislation totally

Atlantic Development Board inadequate for the job it is supposed to handle, and certainly not worthy of being put on the statute books of this nation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Cape Breton South, I will be very short in order that the bill may be given second reading. I listened to the hon. member speaking on the bill, and I have also listened to other speeches he has made in the house. He says he cannot understand why some of the officials of APEC, a well known body which was referred to by the hon. member for Gloucester as a commendable organization in the Atlantic provinces, are in favour of setting up such a board because in his view it is nothing but a subterfuge.
I have not been in this house long, and the hon. member has not been here as long as I have. May I simply say that he has said some things which are helpful, but he must realize that there are many wise men in APEC from all over the maritime provinces and that they are looking at this matter in an objective manner and giving their opinion on it. I should like to quote from the New Glasgow News of November 15 last in which there is a report on what the new president of APEC had to say about the setting up of the Atlantic development board:
Gerald E. Martin, in his first public address since assuming presidency of the self-help regional organization last month, said creation of the board would mark the first entrance of the federal government into direct area development. He cautioned against thinking the board could do the entire job of encouraging regional development by itself.
The article goes on to indicate that Mr. Martin put forward various matters which have already been mentioned in this house by way of suggestions to be made to the new board by APEC.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate spoke yesterday, and the hon. member for Gloucester spoke on the resolution. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate set himself up as the spokesman for the Atlantic provinces, the one who knows all about these matters. Let me just say there are those of us in the house who are natives of the Atlantic provinces and who feel we can speak as well for this area as the hon. member, who has moved to Newfoundland and has actually been adopted by that province.
During the last few years the hon. member for Gloucester has been the opposition coal critic in the house, but from the speech of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate yesterday it would appear that he and the member for Gloucester are now the friends of the fishermen. Apparently the hon. member for Gloucester is no longer the coal critic
[Mr. Maclnnis.l

but has now moved into another field. The hon. member made quite a lengthy speech, which I do not intend to go into because it was made at another stage of the legislation and was referred to by the hon. member for Cumberland.
I should like to refer to a few of the matters mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I remember as a young boy and probably in later years going to afternoon movie matinees. Yesterday afternoon we witnessed another matinee performance by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He put on quite a show. I listened attentively to all his speech. I think the only thing he said which would be of assistance and could be taken as a good suggestion for the Atlantic development board or to help the Atlantic provinces was when he put forward certain things that the board should study.
He admitted in his remarks that when he was a member of the former government when it was in power more should have been done in the field of defence production, in getting more work from that department for the Atlantic area. We also have been trying to do that and perhaps I could point out a few ways in which the Department of Defence Production, under the able minister, has been able to help out in my own constituency.
For instance, a variable depth sonar has been developed, one of the best known antisubmarine devices in the world. We have not only used this device in our Royal Canadian Navy, but we have sold it to the Royal Navy and the Royal Australian Navy, and I believe the Department of Defence Production is attempting to sell it to the United States. This variable depth sonar is manufactured by
E.M.I. Cossor Limited at Dartmouth, and subcontracts have been let to companies in other communities including Fairey Aviation at Dartmouth and Trenton Industries Limited in my constituency.
As I understand it, since 1957 industries in my own area and undoubtedly in other parts of the Atlantic provinces have been listed with various government departments for material which can be supplied, and have been able to secure contracts. At Trenton Industries they are making mortar carriers for the Department of Defence Production as well as the towing gear for the variable depth sonar.
In my area, and this affects all areas in the Atlantic provinces and the shipyards, the following has been carried out by other government departments during the last five years. For instance, right now a coastguard cutter is being built at the Ferguson Industries

Limited yards, Pictou, Nova Scotia, in my constituency. Tenders were called and the three lowest bids included one from the great lakes yards, one from the St. Lawrence area and one from the maritimes area. I suggested to the Minister of Transport that since these vessels would be used in various parts of Canada the work should be allotted on a regional basis. The Ferguson yard at Pictou, being the lowest bidder in the maritimes, was awarded a contract for one of these craft. The other two contracts went to a great lakes yard and a St. Lawrence yard respectively. This was a big help.
I should like also to refer to the ferry constructed about two years ago to operate between Portugal Cove and Belle island, Newfoundland, in the constituency of the hon. member for St. John's East. The call for tenders was limited to the maritime yards, and this was the case with the new ferry which will be constructed during this coming year at the Ferguson Industries Limited yard at Pictou. This ferry will operate between Wood island and Cariboo. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made the suggestion that we should do more to encourage the tourist industry, and I believe the new ferry will help in that direction because there will no longer be a line-up for the ferry at either Wood island or Cariboo.
Then the hon. member pointed out that the board should study our fisheries. I agree with that suggestion. Subsidies were introduced by the Minister of Transport to pay 50 per cent of the cost of construction of steel trawlers. This will be of great assistance to the fishermen. May I point out, sir, that the fisheries school in the province of Nova Scotia is located at Pictou. During the last few months, in order to enlarge the school and make more facilities available for training young fishermen in the Atlantic provinces, the federal government gave approximately $150,000 to help the province of Nova Scotia with this work. I can therefore concur with the hon. member that our fisheries would be a most important subject of study.
The hon. member also pointed out that coal should be used to a greater extent in the production of power in the Atlantic provinces. May I point out to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that if he had travelled from Stellarton to Trenton while he was in my constituency he would have seen the thermal plant at Trenton. The enlargement of this plant was made possible by the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, and between $2 million and $3 million was spent by this government for that purpose. This power, which is generated from coal, was hooked up to the grid system connecting Nova Scotia and New Brunswick,
Atlantic Development Board which was also made possible by the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act. Rates were established for industrial users which were comparable to those in parts of Ontario. Each year these industrial users are given a rebate, which means that at the end of the year they get a cheque for an amount which will reduce their rate to one which is comparable to that of industrial users in Ontario. The plant burns coal from our Pictou county mines.
I believe, therefore, that the board which this bill will establish will help various parts of the Atlantic provinces. Mine is a surplus labour area, but I am not going into the reasons for it being such an area. During the last years some coal mines have closed down, but I am not pointing the finger at anyone for that. Various reasons were behind it. We have a large plant there which makes railway cars. During the last ten years the railways embarked on a program of changes in their rolling stock, and there is not so much need for these railway cars now. However, the plant is going better now because certain branches of the Canada Car Company at Montreal have been moved and now the roofs and ends of these cars are made at Trenton. This plant of the Eastern Car Company gives employment to about 75 men.
I believe that this board, when established, will be able to bring together the various facts and suggestions and give them proper consideration. The provinces in the Atlantic area can get together and make their presentations to the board in the best way possible. It has been suggested that APEC has carried out research in various areas so why go into them again. There are always other things to learn. I feel this board could be a very potent factor in the Atlantic area.
I recall, for instance, that a study was carried out by an official from the Department of Trade and Commerce and an official from the Department of Labour, on my suggestion and the suggestion of the premier of Nova Scotia, in order to try to find employment for miners who have been laid off. A similar study was conducted in the Cape Breton area. I am speaking purely of local conditions at the moment, sir, but it is my hope this board will take the study which was made by these two learned gentlemen and give it proper consideration. I have a copy of that report, which is confidential, and it reveals that in a surplus labour area such as Pictou county there are some of the best workers available. Some of them are trained but others would need training and are capable of being trained.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate pointed out many things the former
2382	HOUSE OF
Atlantic Development Board administration had accomplished, such as Camp Gagetown, the Canso causeway and so on. May I point out some of the things which have been accomplished by the present government. One was a measure to assist our working force through the establishment of a vocational training school in our area. It is now being constructed at Stellarton and will be ready around the first of the year, I am told. This was made possible through a grant of 75 per cent of the cost of construction from this government. It is true that we need other types of industry in an area like this which, as I say, is a surplus labour area. We have a heavy steel industry but we need secondary industry, and I think this ooard could look into the matter of enlarging this area of expansion. For instance, in the Trenton plants there is need for a certain type of hammer which will enable the steel works part of those plants to go into other lines of production.
We must keep the industry we have and we must also look for additional industry. We can do this by extra tax incentives and other measures. We have given some already, but more should be done to give further tax incentives and help secondary industry come into the area. This board could examine the work done by Industrial Estates, the crown company set up by the provincial government which has been able to attract two small industries into my area, and work along with it. One is an Italian knitting plant, which is doing very well. The other, the Canada Envelope Company, will be opening early in the new year. They are the type of plants we need, and this is the type of work which the board should tackle first in order to provide employment in labour surplus areas and elsewhere throughout the Atlantic provinces.
I have already referred to the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act and the grants which this government has given to help provide educational services and roads in the province where I live. At the present time a trans-Canada highway project is being carried out in the New Glasgow-Stellarton area which will cost several millions of dollars and is providing employment. It should help to attract more industry to the industrial area of New Glasgow, and provide necessary roads.
There is not much more I can say before taking my seat, except that the government has not done everything it could for the Atlantic provinces. I frankly admit that, but I have pointed out certain things that have been done and we must continue to fight for other things. The establishment of this board will help us to do that.


References have been made to the terms of the bill, and I think the terms are wide enough to do the necessary work. Let us forget about the wording. Let us forget about amending it. Let us get the board working. The time has come for action. We have carried out certain projects during the last five years; now let us keep matters rolling along. I commend the minister for introducing this legislation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not a debate on the merits of APEC, and accordingly I shall not deal with the remarks, or alleged reaction of that organization to the bill presently before us. I listened very attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou, who has just taken his seat. I found what he had to say very interesting, because what he said was much more specific than what the minister said when speaking on the resolution and on the motion for second reading. I only hope that the kind of projects which the hon. member for Pictou sees hidden in the vague language of this bill are indeed hidden there.
Yesterday the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made a suggestion to the government through the Minister of National Revenue. He suggested that there was a general desire shared by all hon. members to get on with the business of the country in this house, and he recognized the general importance of trying to improve the economic position of the Atlantic area. In view of these two considerations the hon. member proposed that after second reading the bill be sent to one of the standing committees, where this legislation, which after all is the government's principal approach to one of the nation's greatest problems, would receive the careful scrutiny that it undoubtedly deserves. In a committee discussions would proceed easily and proposals would be made. I gather the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) would like to move some amendments to the bill, and the virtues of those amendments could be examined in the committee. Indeed proposals, suggestions and amendments might come from all quarters of the house, and I should hope they would. The Minister of National Revenue must appreciate the merit of this invitation, and I invite him, when concluding this debate, to tell us his reaction to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate.
I do not think there is any doubt that hon. members from the Atlantic area propose to support this motion for second reading but, Mr. Speaker, I for one would be less than frank if I did not express the mixture of uncertainty and disappointment which I felt when I first studied the bill. In the first place

the government does not seem to have appraised accurately the seriousness of the problems of the Atlantic area, or to have appraised accurately the scope of action that will be required to deal efficaciously with these problems. It provides for an unpaid board which is to meet once a year. It is true the chairman is to receive an honorarium of $3,000, and it is also true that the board can meet more frequently, but that is what is laid out in the bill itself, and to me this suggests that this board is not expected to accomplish very much.
In the second place, I do not think the board confronts the general problems of our area head on. We all know what those problems are. They are three in number. First there is the matter of our tariff policy. This is a national question; it is not simply a regional one. We all know that since 1879, no matter what government was in office, we have had a tariff policy that has been highly unfavourable to producers and consumers in the maritime provinces. As I say, this is a matter of national policy, so I do not see how this particular board, which is primarily regional in its focus, will be able to cope with all the national ramifications of a change in our tariff policy.
Mr. Speaker, in case you may think this matter is somewhat irrelevant to the motion for second reading of this bill, let me call to your attention a speech made at Kentville by the Minister of Finance last March. The newspaper report of that speech quoted the minister as saying that if Britain were to join the European common market then Sydney or Glace Bay could, within a lifetime, become as large as present day Toronto. This suggests the intimate connection between matters of trade and tariff policy and prosperity in the maritime and Atlantic area of Canada.
Then there is another general problem which is not confronted head on by this board. That is the matter of transportation. Here again we all know what the situation is. We all know that governments over the years have been concerned with this matter, and indeed went so far as to create a royal commission to look into it. The royal commission reported that by reason of the development of competition, particularly trucking competition, in central Canada the railways are having a tough time making ends meet in the extremities of the country. Consequently they apply for permission to raise their freight rates, but this permission they use to its full extent only in those extremities. Therefore the freight rates go up in the east and the west, and they are kept down in the centre of the country by reason of the

A second matter to which the royal commission referred was the nature of the rate structure. The railways use the old value of service principle in determining freight rates. This, as hon. members know, is a principle which says that a valuable commodity when transported shall pay more than a crude and undeveloped commodity; in other words, raw materials are transported cheaper than refined products. This means it is easier to export from the maritime and Atlantic provinces undeveloped raw goods than the products of secondary industries. In other words our present freight rate structure discourages the development of secondary industries in the Atlantic provinces. The matter of transportation is a great problem. Mr. Speaker, a project for the establishment of another board is brought before us this afternoon.
It sure takes a lot of boards of all kinds to operate the economic machinery of this country, and that, merely because the financial gear is unsound. That is how the old Conservative, Liberal and socialist parties try to cure economic ills, not daring to get to the bottom of the problem. They prefer to come out with ready-made plans rather than go to the source of the economic plight brought about by an obsolete financial system which puts up blockades in every segment of the national economy and prevents the Canadian consumer from buying the goods that are produced.

Atlantic Development Board
However, the bill for the establishment of the Atlantic development board, as put forth by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Flemming), commends itself to us because of the goal it seeks to achieve, that is, to promote to the fullest extent possible the industrial, commercial and agricultural development of the Atlantic regions and, consequently, to ensure the well-being of the people and families who live in those great regions, a great number of which are bound to the population of Quebec by their French origin, their French culture and their French civilization. I take this opportunity to pay special tribute to the whole French-speaking population of those provinces, to whom I send a fraternal greeting.
Last summer I had the privilege of coming into close contact with the best people of New Brunswick and, at the same time, to meet many officials of the APEC. This enabled me to grasp the full importance of the serious economic problems our compatriots in the maritimes have to face in the obsolete framework of liberalism where we are all choking as if we were in strait-jackets.
That situation compels us to adopt serious corrective measures in the Atlantic area, as well as in all the regions of Canada, in order to put a stop to unemployment, hardship and lack of security which are the lot of so many Canadians.
During the last 50 years, scientific and technical developments have completely transformed our means of production, thus upsetting our economic and social system, sowing trouble and confusion in the minds of our contemporaries who persist in believing that the capitalist system of debt money has been created by providence to last as long as the solar system and that any other economic system is inconceivable. Mr. Speaker, that is the great error of some official economists who have forgotten to change with the times.
I wish to advise the hon. members of the house that the economic development of the Atlantic region will never be adequately promoted as long as they believe that we need foreign capital to attain that objective, or that all social capital outlays will have to come from money borrowed at high interest rates or from credit created by commercial banks. Let us leave to the Bank of Canada, through a branch that would be called the "municipal development bank", or, in other words, the "social financing bank", the task of providing all the capital needed to meet the public needs of Canada, and at administrative


cost, while respecting the autonomy of each province and provincial-municipal relations, always in relation to our means of production, in such a way that there will no longer be inflation or deflation of our money, as it happened constantly under the old parties, Liberal and Conservative. It will be possible for the Atlantic area to enjoy a tremendous economic development, and the same will apply to all other provinces in this country, when, through the means I have just advocated, we will allow the savings of our citizens and the capital accumulated in finance institutions to play their part to the full, in all security for those savings and that capital, through investment in the industrial and business fields. In that way, Canadians will regain control of their economy and the Atlantic area will no longer have to suffer economic depression in the midst of extremely rich natural resources.
Since the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) advocated the establishment of a department of the Atlantic with a deputy minister and other officials, I suggest that the government should soon consider establishing such a department to look after the economic development of the socialist province of Saskatchewan.
We, of the Social Credit, would like the Gaspe peninsula and the Saguenay area to be considered as being part of the Atlantic area and we respectfully but strongly suggest that a Quebec representative be appointed on this Atlantic development board.

It is a fact, however, that average incomes in this region continue to lag behind the averages for the rest of Canada. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), as reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of November 3, said that his party could give better government, more progressive government at this critical time. At that same time their new found disciple from Antigonish-Guysborough lamented the fact that Nova Scotia had sent nine Conservatives to the House of Commons. He said that Nova Scotia is traditionally Liberal and is now oppressed by Tory protectionism. What did he say today? He said that this board cannot be expected to accomplish very much. This type of attitude was Liberal party policy for 22 years. "We cannot do very much for the maritimes so we Liberals will do nothing."
I submit it is time to get rid of this pessimistic idea. It is time to look forward, to have a progressive twentieth century outlook for the Atlantic provinces. What do the economic indicators tell us? I do not know where the hon. member goes when he leaves here but it is certainly not back to Nova Scotia because if he did he would be aware of the progress that is being made. The improvement in economic activity in the Atlantic provinces since this government came into office in 1957 is almost astronomical. For years we were dependent upon transfer payments and upon social security and defence expenditures for a large part of our income. However, this type of dependency could not go on indefinitely, and immediately upon taking office we recognized these problems and set about doing something about them. Programs were instituted that were not merely a scratching of the surface but which would be beneficial over a long period of time.
As I said previously, the first thing we did was to bring in the adjustment grants. Armed with this additional capital, the provincial


government of Nova Scotia established industrial estates which promoted new industry. Under our roads to resources program we encouraged the provinces to build new highways, and this has assisted in faster delivery of our fish to the markets in the United States. It has also brought in new tourists and last year we had a tourist season in Nova Scotia greater than we have ever had before in our history. This meant that we required more hotels and motels, and these are springing up all over the province. I ask any Liberal member in this house to stand up and deny that this is a fact.
We encouraged the construction of new technical schools. Unlike the Liberals, who gave no thought to the effects of automation upon our youth, we recognized that they cannot continue untrained and we are making every effort to provide facilities for their technical training so they will be in a position to make a contribution to industry in the future. We provided aid to the production and distribution of power. In fact, last year, for the first time in the history of Nova Scotia, we sold power to the United States where a shortage had developed. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud)-and I listened to his words of wisdom-obviously, has not been back to the Atlantic provinces recently because no one could even fly over them without seeing the neon lights and the blossoming suburbs which indicate that we are forging ahead.
The goal of the Conservative party is to bring about employment opportunities in the Atlantic provinces so that our citizens have jobs at salaries close to the national average. We want to develop our area; we want to stop the drain on our manpower so prevalent for so many years under the Liberals. As I mentioned previously, the measures already enacted have been most helpful. However, I would not have you believe all our problems have been solved. There are still some areas of Nova Scotia that are underdeveloped, areas in the Atlantic provinces that are underdeveloped. This is the result of a lack of employment opportunities.
I would suggest that we might ask this board to give some consideration to the further development of our gypsum deposits, and the processing of them. We can mine two million tons of gypsum per year for 100 years and we would still have some reserves. We have whales going up and down the coast, and we could give some thought to the canning and processing of them. To the best of my knowledge, there is no canning of tuna in the Atlantic provinces anywhere. Now, some hon. member may correct my statement, but I do not believe there is a can of tuna put up in the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island or Newfoundland today. This is one of the products of the sea that is gaining increasing favour with consumers not only in Canada but in the United States.
I would ask the board to start a search for minerals through the new oceanographic institute that has been located on the shores of Bedford basin. They could search for minerals on the shores of our continental shelf. We must carry out a greater search for oil, for gas and for other minerals and actively process them. There are a multitude of jobs the Atlantic development board, when established, could do. I do not go along with the hon. member for Gloucester or the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill) when they criticize this government for not setting the amount this board could .spend. This, I submit, would put a limitation


on the number of projects the board could develop for the assistance of the area. This government will back up the board, I am certain, when the projects it recommends to the treasury board are judged feasible. I am sure this government will back up this board because it has been the intention of our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and of the Conservative government since we were first elected to bring about a better economic standard in the Atlantic provinces. I am sure that we intend to continue bringing this area up to the level of the rest of Canada. However, it is costly to maintain underemployment in any part of Canada, including the Atlantic provinces. It will be the purpose of this board to correct this situation.
What we need are policies which are aimed at the creation of new production, employment and new income. In the long run, this will be beneficial not only to the people of the Atlantic provinces but to Canadians as a whole. Another project to which this board could give consideration would be the production of cranberries. In Cape Cod they have made this a major industry. Here in Ottawa, you buy cranberries packaged and processed in Cape Cod. Cranberries grow well in all areas of the Atlantic provinces. This is a project to which consideration might well be given by this board in an effort to stimulate our economy.
I am in agreement with one thing which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate stated-I note he is not here today-namely his suggestion that we might take a closer look at our traditional markets in the West Indies. I believe the hon. member for Gloucester also mentioned this.
The volume of business between Canada and the British Caribbean is showing a steady growth and our commercial relations continue to be governed by the Canada West Indies trade agreement of 1926 which provides for the exchange of preferential tariff treatment. Our economies are complementary and there is a geographical proximity to the Atlantic provinces. With improved transportation and communications, plus the flow of Canadian tourists, trade missions and our Canadian assistance program there is no reason why we should not increase our long established trade with Trinidad, Tobago, Barbados, Jamaica and the Windward and Leeward Islands.
Last year we imported over $84 million worth of goods from the West Indies while we exported only $56 million worth, so there is quite a difference in our trade balance. Clearly it is up to us in the Atlantic provinces to stimulate further the sales of our fish, lumber, newsprint, tinned milk, potatoes,

onions, apples and paper products, all of which are grown and processed in the Atlantic provinces and which would greatly improve our employment opportunities if we increased our sales.
I am certain the Atlantic development board will be beneficial to our area and, working together with the leaders of our provincial governments and established industries it will bring about a more stable economy and a higher standard of living for all our people. At this point I would like to pay a tribute to Mr. Michael Waddell of the Atlantic Advocate for the time and effort he has put into dealing with Atlantic region problems. I have read his editorials and comments and he has devoted space in his periodical to bring our needs not only to the attention of maritimers but to all of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have no wish to get into the family quarrel between the various members from the Atlantic provinces on both sides of the house. A long time ago I learned that when you get into a family quarrel you usually get into trouble. For three days I have listened to Liberal members claiming that the Conservatives did not do anything and are largely responsible for conditions in the maritimes, and I have listened to Conservative members blaming the Liberals for their long period of inactivity. I think it is easy for me to keep out of trouble by saying I agree that both are right. The problems of the maritimes, whether they are understated or overstated are due to the fact that both old-line parties, both provincially and federally, have had the responsibility of looking after the affairs of the Atlantic provinces ever since Canada became a nation.
I would like to commend the Minister of National Revenue for introducing legislation to set up an Atlantic economic development board. I do so for two reasons, the first being that I think we recognize today, somewhat belatedly, that economic planning is absolutely essential if our economy is going to get moving and if we are going to grapple with the problems of unemployment and a low standard of living, low compared to the potential which we might enjoy.
I am glad to have this legislation brought down for a second reason, and that is that it is particularly aimed at the problems of the Atlantic provinces and, as I said in the debate on the resolution, those provinces deserve special consideration and need special action. I think the house will generally agree with the minister in having legislation designed to do that; however I want to say to the minister that all the fears I expressed in the debate on the resolution have been more than justified after reading the terms of the bill. Having read the bill I cannot help but feel that the mountain has laboured and brought forth a mouse and that this legislation will not do the things that many of the hon. members have been talking about.
I have listened to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan) talking about the employment which this board will create, and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. 

Crouse), who has just resumed his seat, talking about the new industrial development that could be brought about. But I cannot see anything in this bill that is either going to provide employment or bring into being new industries or a greater development of the resources of the Atlantic provinces. I say that for three reasons, Mr. Speaker. First of all I look at the board itself. Here is a board of five members, of which there is not to be a single full time member. Whether this board is going to meet once a year, quarterly or even monthly, surely no one in his right senses thinks a part time board meeting periodically is going to produce the kind of program that we need to make a massive assault on the social and economic problems of the Atlantic provinces. There is not even a full time chairman. I agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pick-ersgill) who suggested, much along the same line as the suggestion I made with reference to the national economic development board, that if you are going to tie this board into the government the chairman ought to be a minister of the crown. If that is too much to ask, then at least he should be a parliamentary secretary.
I am really disturbed by this feeble bow we in this parliament are making to the idea of economic planning. We are now going to have four planning groups. We are going to have the national economic development board, the Atlantic development board, an enlarged national productivity council and an industrial manpower adjustment council, all four of them with terms of reference which are overlapping, all of them responsible to a different minister, and none of them tied in to the government so that their recommendations and programs have any assurance of being considered.
The other thing that worries me about this board is this. With only five members it cannot possibly be representative of (a) regions, and (b) major economic groups. I would like to see a board on which the provinces concerned will be represented by allowing them to nominate someone, and the major economic groups being allowed to nominate someone who will represent them. I do not mean by this, selecting someone from an economic group, but someone nominated by an economic group who will have the authority to confer with that group and, with their agreement, commit that group to certain lines of action. If we are really going to plan the economic development of the Atlantic provinces we will have to have this kind of representation, co-ordination and participation by the various groups concerned. That is certainly not possible with a board of five part time members.

I want to hurry along, Mr. Speaker, because I do not want to hold up this bill. The second thing that concerns me about this bill is the limited scope of the board. It has the power to make an assessment of the factors relevant to economic growth; it has the power to decide whether or not certain measures, projects and existing factors may inhibit industrial development; it has power-this is what worries me most-to study particular measures or projects if they are referred to it by the minister. We have heard a great deal about the projects they will discuss, but as I read this bill they cannot discuss or make a study of any projects unless they are projects which have been referred to them by the minister. If I am wrong, or if this requires some clarification, we can discuss it in the committee. But it seems to me that is a limitation which means this board could do virtually nothing, or it could do a considerable amount if projects are referred to it; although what five people meeting several times a year can do is beyond my understanding.

This point is very well set out in the sixteenth edition of Sir Erskine May's work on parliamentary practice at page 461. There is a paragraph there dealing with law officers' opinions, and we find this stated;
The opinions of the law officers of the crown, being confidential, are not usually laid before parliament or cited in debate; and their production has frequently been refused:
Then if we turn to page 270 we find this:
Parliament is invested with the power of ordering all documents to be laid before it, which are necessary for its information. Each house enjoys this authority separately, but not in all cases independently of the crown.

Accounts and papers relating to trade, finance, and general or local matters, are ordered directly, and are returned in obedience to the order of the house whence it was issued: but returns of matters connected with the exercise of the royal prerogative, are obtained by means of addresses to the crown.
The distinction between these two classes of returns should be borne in mind; as, on the one hand, it is irregular to order directly that which should be sought for by address; and, on the other, it is a compromise of the authority of parliament to resort to the crown for information which it can obtain by its own order. The application of the principle is not always clear: but, as a general rule, it may be stated that all public departments connected with the collection or management of the revenue, or which are under the control of the treasury, or are constituted or regulated by statute, may be reached by a direct order from either house of parliament: but that public officers and departments, subject to Her Majesty's secretaries of state or the privy council, are to receive their orders from the crown.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to speak about Bill C-94, to provide for the establishment of an Atlantic development board, but since several members who have already spoken on this matter mentioned the area I represent, namely the Saguenay district, I feel bound to make a few comments.
Mr. Speaker, the bill now under discussion provides for the establishment of another board to study the Atlantic area which includes, according to some hon. members, the maritime provinces, Newfoundland and the ridings of Saguenay and of the Gaspe peninsula.
I should like to point out, first of all, that there are already in the areas mentioned of the province of Quebec, two bodies concerned with regional economic studies, namely the

lower St. Lawrence economic council and the gulf and lower St. Lawrence development organization, which perform at present the same duties as the board proposed in the bill now under consideration.
Mr. Speaker, I am not against the establishment of such a board to serve the district that I represent; I am all for it. But, although I agree with the principle of the bill, I cannot accept it in its present wording.
It is proposed to create a five member board, only the chairman of which will be paid $3,000 a year.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider the region that this council will serve, from an economic as well as a geographical standpoint, we realize that it will not be able to be effective, since its means are limited. In my opinion, what should be established is an economic council which would include those who already exist and which would have a budget enabling it to offer adequate salaries to its officials, its chairman, secretary and any other, in order to cover that territory. Because with $3,000, no one would succeed in covering even half of it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, while I am in favour of the principle of the bill, I do not agree with its substance, and, on third reading, I might have amendments to submit to make it more efficient.
If the Saguenay, lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe areas are incorporated in the bill, changes which have not been considered by the hon. members will have to be made to the work program of the board.
In the first place, there is the matter of a bridge across the Saguenay river. There lies the greatest obstacle to the development of the north shore. Everybody is of the opinion that such a bridge would cost $25 million. Then, there is the urgent need of a highway between the Saguenay area and Blanc Sablon. Such a road should go straight to Newfoundland by means of a causeway across the strait of Belle Isle.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, the development of the north shore is hampered by the lack of communication between the areas. The highway does not go beyond Sept lies and there is another 600 miles to Blanc Sablon, the point nearest to Newfoundland.
It is essential that this board be able to take effective steps to have a road built in co-operation with the Department of National Defence because such a road would be
Atlantic Development Board used for the defence of North America since it would serve the whole eastern part of the province of Quebec.
The causeway to link Blanc Sablon to Newfoundland, advocated by a professor at the agricultural school of St. Anne de la Pocatiere, would improve the climate in the province of Quebec, for as he said, experts have found that if that causeway were built, the temperature would gain a few degrees, which would be an asset for agriculture since the farming season could begin earlier and last longer, particularly in the Gaspe peninsula and on the north shore.
Another undertaking that should be added to the program of that board is the construction of a railway between La Malbaie and Sept lies. At the present time, there is no railway linking that region to the rest of the province.
Mr. Speaker, it might be said in reply that water transportation is cheaper than rail transportation, but it has been proven that railways stimulate the development of underdeveloped regions.
In my opinion, the government must recognize the principle that communications must exist before economic development can be achieved, and that it is not the other way around. The government has to take the necessary action with regard to communications in that region of the province.
Some kind of planning is required within the government itself. I do not know if that is socialism, but as a start there should be planning of the government itself, planning of the activities of the various departments, in the same way as we are trying to plan the economic development of this country.
Governmental activities have always followed the economic development in a given area. The government is forced by companies to establish means of communications, once the industries themselves are established. Both provincial and federal governments are forced to establish communications, so that industries can remain in touch with the rest of the province.
That is the first kind of planning the government should establish. I must say here that we have before us now a government which is trying to set up what I would describe as mitigated planning. It wants to plan and, at the same time, it doesn't want to; it is in favour of the principles of planning without actually planning.

Atlantic Development Board
I should prefer a government which would say exactly what it has in mind. We could then mount a frontal attack against it.
As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) said this afternoon, there are four commissions whose functions are overlapping, while it would be much better to have only one which would direct its activities where they could be the most effective.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I had not prepared myself for a long speech. I do not want to delay the proceedings of the house, but I should like to say that I endorse the principle of the bill. However, I may take the liberty of introducing an amendment on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting to listen to the hon. member for Saguenay (Mr. Maltais) who just took his seat, and to observe how, with such great affection, he embraced a part of the socialist program. Perhaps he should communicate those ideas to his co-leaders on the front benches in order that they may get on the right track or the wrong track, as the case may be.
I wish generally to indicate our support for the bill itself at this stage. While I come from the other part of the country, namely the Pacific coast, none the less since I have been here not only during these last few days but in previous sessions, as have some other hon. members who are not immediately familiar with the situation in the Atlantic provinces, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the problems which have been related to parliament by members coming from those provinces. While only on three occasions have I had the opportunity to visit two of the Atlantic provinces, none the less I think that all hon. members, although we may not actually have been in contact with those provinces at all in a physical way, appreciate greatly the difficulties which have existed there for a long period of time. We have heard in this house many pleas by members from those areas with regard to the high levels of unemployment which have existed over the past many years, including not only those since June of 1957 but many prior to that time.
We have heard and read a great deal about the so-called runaway industries which leave the maritimes or the Atlantic area in order to relocate or to open plants in southern Ontario, and thus leave behind them a group of people who are unemployed. We have heard a great deal about industries being closed. I refer to the coal mines and the
steel industry. We have heard about the difficulties encountered in the fishing industry and the like. We have an understanding of and a sympathy with those difficulties, if only in a vicarious way, having listened to members in years past and now notably to my colleague from Cape Breton South, explaining the problems which exist there.
Without being unkind in any way I think we could perhaps say that the Atlantic provinces, as a geographic area in Canada, are perhaps, as they have been for some time in the past, the most depressed area in Canada, or the one which has the greatest economic difficulties and the highest continuing levels of unemployment, without the possibility of those people who are unemployed finding gainful employment. Having regard to these conditions which have prevailed and worsened over the years, it is rather sad in one sense to listen to these two old blind parties, one in government and the other hopefully expectant of getting there, rail against each other as being the cause of these economic difficulties.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
Yes; it does sound like that. I cannot think of a party better qualified to be in mourning than the Liberal party. The sad part of it is that for as long as there have been governments in those provinces, they have been either of one or the other party. Unfortunately, also, for as long as there have been governments in Canada, they have been either of one or the other party. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, who spoke before the supper hour, said in reference to each blaming the other, each finds itself in agreement with the other. There was recognition-speaking from memory I believe it was perhaps in 1953-when the present Minister of Forestry and Minister of National Revenue was premier of one of those provinces, when steps were taken, exploratory at first, but eventually to establish what is known as the Atlantic provinces economic council which consisted then, as it consists now, of people representing business and industry and with the sanction and blessing of the governments in those provinces. Undoubtedly this step was necessitated by the fact that those provinces and the people in them found themselves in increasingly greater and more difficult economic circumstances. As a result, as economic conditions became so bad, even the governments, reluctant as they might have been, were forced into a recognition of the necessity of

dealing with this question of the economy of the Atlantic provinces by way of government intervention or government activity.
Ever since I heard of it or read of it the Atlantic provinces economic council has intrigued me. I have read something of the studies which it has undertaken and the things which it has proposed. If I may do so, I should like to make a brief reference to one of the publications issued in January of this year entitled, "Incentives for manufacturing industry". Perhaps in that way, using the words of this council itself, I can bring hon. members to appreciate why we endorse the concepts contained within this particular bill. Even though it has failures in it, even though at a subsequent stage we may make specific reference to parts of the bill which we think are a little bit weak, none the less, perhaps by referring to the Atlantic provinces economic council and its proposals we can come to understand why this is in fact a step in the direction of planning, the socialist concept which we in the New Democratic party and those previously in the C.C.F. have advocated for so many years, and which finally is coming to be accepted even by our friends in the Social Credit party who espouse just the opposite point of view. Let me read first from this booklet-and these are not my words, my ideas or the ideas of the New Democrats but the ideas of the Atlantic provinces economic council, the ideas of industry in these provinces, of free enterprise and of the political parties forming the governments in these provinces. They have this to say:
A development program for Canada's four eastern provinces must be bold, massive and well coordinated. Governments must take the initiative-
This is a plea, if you will, on the part of the so-called free enterprisers and free enterprise parties for government control, government regulation, government initiative, government intervention. I continue the quotation:
-and it is imperative that the federal government be active in formulating, financing and administering a regional development program.
It goes on to make reference to the necessity of the federal government establishing a capital fund to assist in making what they call basic improvements in the capital structure both in the public and the private sectors. They make reference to the necessity of having a system of loans and grants for the purchase and acquisition of industrial machinery and equipment. They go into the field of transportation assistance and refer also to adequate vocational and technical programs to equip labour with the necessary skills and the like. Throughout page after
Atlantic Development Board page of this booklet they make such recommendations and plead for government intervention, government regulation and government co-ordination of the activities there in order to provide circumstances as a result of which the economy of that part of the country will be raised again to a decent level.
They talk throughout of the necessity for federal participation and how essential it is for the federal government to participate in financing, research, regional development and so on. Some of the latter words of this booklet have to do with the assessment of situations. They talk about selecting industries for assistance. Let me read a word or two from this part:
In all cases, however, an assessment will have to be made of each applicant industry's prospect for success. Assistance should be restricted to those industries, and those firms, which have reasonable prospects of operating successfully, without assistance, after a period of time.
That is a direct plea for government regulation, government co-ordination. They go on to say:
In addition, assisted industries should be those that would form part of the economic base of the region and should not include service industries, such as retail establishments and financial institutions, and those industries whose growth proceeds automatically with increases in population.
They are advocating a selective program of government assistance and government regulation and intervention. I could read many other quotations from this particular document issued in January of this year, but I think those few should be sufficient to indicate that even the so-called free enterprisers in business themselves, even the political parties in the Atlantic provinces, as reluctant, right wing and reactionary as they may be, have come to the conclusion by reason of terrible economic circumstances that government must get into this particular field and offer assistance. This is precisely what we have been saying for many years, and in the face of the most violent opposition not too many years ago. This appears odd indeed to me; but while, as I said, the bill is weak in some cases and while we will attempt to draw these weaknesses to the attention of the committee when we reach the particular clauses, nevertheless it is a basic step in the direction of planning, co-ordinating and assisting from the government level in the economic development of a section of this country.
When I listened to the Liberals opposing this bill-we will know better whether they are opponents when it comes to a vote-condemning it upside down and this way and that, and condemning the government for bringing it in while at the same time saying that the government stole it from their own program, it makes me wonder how much lack

Atlantic Development Board of truth there can be in one political party. As I said earlier, as far as I am concerned the bill warrants our support and endorsa-tion, and we hope we can correct the weaknesses at a later stage.

For many, many years, actually for centuries, the Atlantic provinces have been known for their mines, their forest resources, their fruit and vegetable production and the production of fish. Most industries that have developed over the years have been connected with these natural resources. Now that these natural resources have been used up the people in communities dependant on these resources are now faced with the problem of continuing their existence and they cannot do this without government assistance, without the assistance provided by a measure such as we are talking about tonight. It seems to me this is a proper method of handling the problem.
I do believe if we are going to establish this board, then we should be prepared to put the necessary money into it to ensure its success. We have in Canada, and on the North American continent as a whole, developed our industries around two or three major areas. There has been, as a result, a rush to increase the concentration of these industries. This has proven to be detrimental to most of the outside areas of our country. Our country is still a very large, unpopulated nation and because of this it has been difficult to get the consumption of our goods in the areas of production. There has been a tendency, of course, to put our major manufacturing industries into three main centres, and that has been detrimental to the other areas.
I am very interested, Mr. Speaker, in seeing some success achieved in the maritimes. I am interested in this because only then will it be possible to develop the area that I represent. This area now faces a problem which the maritimes has had for many years. We hear a great deal about the displacement of labour in the maritime coal mines and in other industries, and that is what is taking place in many other areas of Canada. In my own riding, we are faced with a large number of lay-offs every year as a result of the closing of some mines. Many of our communities were built upon non-renewable resources, and they are faced with the problem of either becoming ghost towns or finding some form of government assistance that will provide the necessary capital to enable the necessary research to be conducted to develop other industries.
It seems to me that in the maritimes they have waited a long time for this type of development. The maritimes have developed

He has been very interested over the years in the Atlantic provinces economic council. Here, for the first time, we have an organization developed by the people themselves to help themselves. They are now coming to the federal government for assistance. I certainly hope we will give them whatever assistance is necessary.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why we have to have this piece of legislation on a regional basis. I am not sure that the national economic development board could not have provided on a national basis what we are trying to do through this board on a regional basis. We, in the New Democratic party, have always said we could supply the economic planning necessary to take care of all parts of Canada, as well as any other assistance that was necessary for the equal development of all parts of our country. I still believe that this can be done. I wonder why it has not been possible for the present Conservative government to do this, to introduce a measure, national in scope, such as we are demanding for the Atlantic region, so that this type of assistance could be extended to all the underdeveloped parts of our nation. We will build a nation, Mr. Speaker, despite the actions of some of the entrepreneurs in this country, despite some of our governments who are giving away our national resources. I suggest we can and will eventually do this. I further suggest that the establishment of the Atlantic development board will act as a guidepost for other areas, and in fact for all parts of Canada which are faced with problems similar to those found in the Atlantic region. We hope that this board will be a success and bring industries to the maritimes to enable them to establish a healthy economy.
I hope the government will not hesitate to provide the necessary money from the treasury to see that this is done. If it is done then we will build this country from coast to coast, and we will also do what the hon. member for Saguenay (Mr. Maltais) suggested, namely, increase our transportation and communication systems so that we will have a united nation from coast to coast. If the establishment of this board will in any way hasten the day when all Canada will find itself able to avail itself of the type of resources provided by national governments in most countries of the world, then the house can be assured of our support for this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on second reading of Bill C-94, an act to provide for the establishment of an Atlantic development board.
I did not think it proper for some hon. members, when discussing this bill to unearth old political quarrels, buried in the past, in order to blame such and such administration for the unfortunate conditions which are now prevailing in our maritime provinces.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Our past should rather be a springboard to the future.
We remember that, at the time of confederation, the maritime provinces had to give up a great part of their sovereignty and of their foreign markets.
Confederation was at that time and perhaps is, even now, an historic structure defying every economic and geopolitical principle of the day. According to geography and economics at that time, a vertical, north-south trade was much more appropriate than a horizontal one from the Atlantic provinces to the west.
The Atlantic provinces therefore sacrificed part of their natural trade to form a great nation.
From the point of view of national pride, that sacrifice had marvellous results. The provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and more recently Newfoundland, are proud of having contributed to the formation and development of our Canadian heritage.
However, from an economic point of view, the maritimes made the greatest sacrifice, and a very costly sacrifice it was. The natural laws of trade gradually channelled prosperity towards the geographical centre of the nation, forsaking the Atlantic area.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that a large part of our population in the maritimes has to find its subsistence in those three marginal activities that are small scale farming, fishing and logging. This means that a great number of our people must be, at the same time, farmers, fishermen and lumberjacks.
In the commercial and industrial fields, lack of capital and distance, which means transportation costs, paralyse our development.
We are familiar with our own problems and the important thing is to find some solution for them.
Though it was ridiculous, yesterday and today, to claim in the house that certain political parties had done nothing for the maritime provinces since confederation, it

would be no less ridiculous to maintain tonight that the bill before us will bring about a lasting, final, total and complete solution of all our problems.
This bill alone is not the key which will open the door to prosperity for us, but it may help us find the way. Therefore, it deserves our consideration. First of all, two principles should be established.
First, the establishment of the Atlantic development board should not be just an excuse to delay basic and urgent action concerning the immediate needs of the maritimes.
Second, this bill should not be just a smoke-screen to hide the activities of the government and get a few more votes at the next election, as seems to have been the case with the construction of the causeway, in Prince Edward Island, which was promised last spring.
A number of questions come to our mind and we should like to have answers from the minister in that connection.
In the first place, we should like to know exactly what authority the board will have. Its terms of reference seem rather vague. Will it be just another board like the others which have been set up from coast to coast, in Canada, to give to the government advice which is disregarded and which does not produce any results.
If this organization is simply going to do research work and give advice to the government, then, we already have one with similar functions, namely APEC.
There is also the matter of salary. It seems to me that in giving a $3,000 salary to the chairman of that board, we do not give a great importance to the said board particularly when we realize that the president of the C.N.R. is paid $75,000. Very well, Mr. Speaker, I will deal only with the principle of the bill.
I wanted to give an example in order to establish the difference that can exist sometimes between the application of a principle and that principle itself. Here is what I was driving at. There is talk about a development board, but in an economy, according to the very definition of any political economy program or system, three problems must be dealt with, namely production, exchange and consumption.
I understand that the purpose of the bill under study is to make it possible for the economy of the Atlantic provinces to develop without help. To reach that objective, the production system itself must function. And my example would have shown that in order for the production system to function, there must be also a consumption system. Now, that consumption system can be either domestic or foreign, but it remains that a consumption system is needed next to the production system.
About this bill providing for the development of the maritime provinces, here is my suggestion to the Minister of National Revenue. It is possible to develop production systems in the maritime provinces, but only if a parallel consumption system is also established. There is no doubt that the necessary steps can be taken to develop a productive economy in the maritime provinces, and on a large scale, if you have the consumers.

It is also possible to develop a farm production system in the maritimes along with a consumption system.
Mr. Speaker, any economic system must have three correlated sectors-production, exchange and consumption.
Therefore, if the economy of the Atlantic provinces is to develop at the same rate as in the other provinces, it should also have not only a system of production but also a system of planned consumption as a production factor. And in order for the bill presented today by the Minister of National Revenue to be effective and to reach the intended objective, the board will have to take into consideration, first and foremost, the whole system of exchange of products in order to enable the consumers to get the production which will develop in the maritime provinces. The Atlantic development board will then reach its objective which is to develop the whole economy of the maritime provinces, the economy of production, exchange and consumption in these four provinces, which really need it.
Mr. Speaker, the major problem in the maritimes is consumption. As soon as the consumers in the Atlantic provinces receive help, the production system will become adequate in those provinces. In fact, if we seriously intend to bring about the economic development of the maritimes, and, at the same time, to give prosperity to the consumers, the whole economic system of those provinces will have to be taken into consideration.

I think it would be a mistake if it were interpreted by the people of the Atlantic region that the setting up of this board is going to bring about any substantial change in the economic forces that have been at work in the Atlantic region for so many years. As I see it, the economic problem of the Atlantic region is not an isolated problem. I think it would be a mistake if this board were to approach it in that manner. The problem of the Atlantic region is, in a sense, the problem of Canada. Certain economic forces have produced certain results, and if we are going to get different results, then we must in some way modify the economic forces that are at work.
Now, these forces have been referred to during the debate on second reading and specific examples have been given. One force has been the lack of development of our natural resources. This, of course, is related to the matter of capital investment. If we are going to do anything about this, it does not seem that the government requires any special advice because one of the things that has inhibited the growth of the Atlantic provinces has been the tax policies followed by federal governments over the years. Unless we are prepared to do something about that, then we cannot hope to make any substantial improvement in the capital investment picture so far as this particular region is concerned.

We all know that the problem of hydro power in Quebec was connected with the tax policy of the federal government, which required substantial payments of income taxes from the province to the federal government. Whatever profits were made, therefore, did not benefit the province at all but went to enrich the federal treasury.
