It is not necessary to wait for a board to be set up for the federal government to take the necessary action to improve the system of communications and the public services in the Atlantic provinces, to put them on a level that will make it attractive for private enterprise to go in and develop industries.
Then, too, we can do more than has been done about encouraging the investment of private capital and discouraging the closing down of industries. A few days ago I had occasion to be in the maritime commission with one of my constituents who was interested in getting a subsidy for a coastal ship. The subject we were concerned with was the Canadian content of this vessel. There are very few companies in Canada today making a diesel engine of around 400 or 500 horsepower for marine installations. I made the remark that I recalled a very fine engine used to be built in British Columbia under the name of Vivian. The expert at the maritime commission said, "Oh, yes, I know all about that; that was a wonderful engine". I said, "Why don't we get one of them?" He said what had happened was that a certain company came in, bought this firm up and then closed it down. This has been the experience

in the maritimes over and over again. Our people have managed to get small businesses going. They have built them up into profitable enterprises and as soon as they have become paying propositions, as soon as they became competitive with comparable enterprises in other parts of Canada, somebody buys them up and closes them down. We had a small tobacco factory in St. John's that used to manufacture tobacco and cigarettes. We were not in confederation three months before the plant was closed down. This is the sort of thing that goes on, and it must be stopped.
I do not envisage very many large scale enterprises in the maritime provinces. I think it is sounder economy if we can establish a number of small enterprises than if we have two or three very large ones. I would much rather have 100 enterprises employing 50 people each than have one enterprise employing 5,000 people.
The other problems we have is that of a domestic market. It is something we cannot do very much about. The government can do what it can by way of freight rate subsidies to equalize freight costs, but under present circumstances it is very difficult to work out a system that is very satisfactory. Somehow or another we must make up for that deficiency. This means that if we cannot have a domestic market in our own region, then the logical place to look for a market is overseas.
My colleague from Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned the Caribbean, which is a logical market for the maritimes; but there are other markets overseas in Europe and we should try to encourage European firms to establish branches in the maritimes from where they can service the American seaboard. If Volkswagen cars were being manufactured in the maritimes they could be distributed right up to central Canada much more cheaply than they are at present.
In my area we have a large market for small motors. We have a big fishing population and diesel motors are becoming very popular as they are economical to operate. We have trade connections with Japan, Norway, Sweden and Germany, countries which are experts in these fields and surely we could induce firms from those countries to establish branches somewhere in the Atlantic region. We must do something of that nature because the possibility of improving our economy solely by exporting our raw materials does not seem to be very effective.
Underlying the economic causes which we see on the surface there is a more basic and deeper cause which we must recognize if we are to understand the nature of the
Atlantic Development Board problem that faces the Atlantic area. As I said before, the problem of the maritimes is the problem of Canada. The problem of underdeveloped areas everywhere in Canada is practically the same. The reasons for underdevelopment are not greatly different from those that prevail in the Atlantic area, and the main reason is really the human factor. It boils down to the motives that make us do the things we do.
I am not against profits, and any firm in business must make profits. If it does not, it cannot have capital to reinvest and expand. That is imperative; but there is another factor which must come into play and that is the duty of a commercial enterprise to assume certain responsibility for the people of the region in which it is established. We cannot have a better example of that than Cuba. Millions and millions of dollars were invested in Cuba and to all intents and purposes they have now disappeared. The main reason was that enterprises established in Cuba spent so much of their energy in producing better and better balance sheets and paid so little attention to their responsibilities toward the people of that country.
This board must recognize that factor. While the economic factors are important, the human factor is equally important. A little jealousy between members of the board can easily disrupt it, or jealousy between this board and other boards can disrupt the relationships between them and nullify the best of plans.
There is one other point I would like to make and it is that while the economic factor cannot be ignored it should not always be the determining factor. All of us have experienced instances where projects that were not economically sound somehow prospered, and of other cases where enterprises had good economic bases and still did not work out. A few weeks ago I had the pleasure of paying a visit to Saskatchewan, through the courtesy of my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar, and the south Saskatchewan development association, and looking at the dam being built there. From an economic standpoint perhaps that dam should never have been built and perhaps it will never justify itself economically, but whether it does or not that is not the point I want to make.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has a right to speak about the economic problems of the maritimes but not about the problems of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not talking about Saskatchewan. I am only using that as an example of a project which perhaps was questionable from the economic standpoint but nevertheless was one that possibly should

Atlantic Development Board have been proceeded with long ago. The reason it was not was that we placed too much emphasis on economic factors and not enough emphasis on the actual needs of the people of the area. Therefore I would ask that we should not let ourselves always be guided completely by whatever economic factors may be involved.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am just a shy, poor old maritimer who has waited two or three days to put a thought on the record and I think it will come under this item, since it has no general application to any of the clauses. This thought comes to my mind. I do not have any amendment to suggest, but it seems important that we have some method of directing the various departments of the federal government to compile statistics and co-operate with the projects that may begin under clause 9 of this bill. I have a very concrete example of this. One of the projects that has been mentioned by others outside this house, and I feel it should have top priority, would be consideration in the future of the ports of Halifax and Saint John in the light of opening up navigation in the St. Lawrence in the winter time. I speak of Saint John from my own personal interest and I am sure the other hon. members from Halifax will agree with me when I say that we are very worried about the future of these maritime ports.
It has been brought to my attention that one of the main difficulties in assessing this problem is the need for co-operation of different departments of government in making available the statistics as to the origin and destination of all traffic in and out of the St. Lawrence system. This is to my mind the main requirement in order to assess the problem in so far as Saint John and Halifax are concerned. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I put that thought forward in connection with the first clause of this bill. I hope the minister will have an opportunity to think about it. As I say, I do not have a specific amendment to put forward. I cannot see how it could be mentioned particularly in the bill. But certainly there will be a necessity as these projects go forward to obtain, not only from the various departments of the federal government but from all other sources, statistics and information, technical and otherwise, that is now available. That is my thought on this matter, Mr. Chairman, and I have related it to a very concrete example.
This project should have top priority in considering the future of Halifax and Saint John in the light of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence and I would hope there would be some method by which those responsible could

direct the Department of Transport and the Department of National Revenue to make available all information provided it was not of a confidential nature. I say that for the benefit of the hon. member for Essex East. I do suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this information would be of great assistance in assessing our problem.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, at this juncture I only desire to pose a question to the minister, a question which involves someone who I understand is an ally of the minister and of his party, someone who, though being a staunch Conservative may not know exactly what his role is within that party. I would ask the minister whether it is the intention, in view of the presence in Ottawa today of this gentleman, to appoint Brigadier Wardell as the chairman of this board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would first like to say that I appreciate the opportunity of making a few remarks on clause 1 of this bill. Before calling the minister's attention to some of the problems which exist in the part of the Atlantic provinces from which I come I would like to make a brief remark concerning his comments on enthusiasm. If I have failed up till now to express great enthusiasm, it is not at all because I disagree with the principle of the bill, but because I began to visualize the government appointing commission after commission, board after board, until a whole host of subgovernments usurped the position of government, and instead of having members elected to the House of Commons computer machines would be installed here to assess the value of the information fed into them by boards. To me that is a horrible thought. Certainly the chamber would not be nearly as interesting as it is today, and apart from that I do not think the public would be too enthusiastic about voting for one or other make of computer machine.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: It would be an improvement in certain areas.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
No doubt my hon. friend knows conditions in his own district. If I might comment on some of the things the board might consider, I would like the minister to think of the potential in wood in Labrador. I am sure that when I mention forestry I am talking to a minister who is not only knowledgeable but sympathetic to this industry. The huge potential of wood in Labrador is something which should be looked at very carefully, and the possibility of constructing roads through the woodlands of Labrador is one which could bear looking into. The minister mentioned earlier the development of forestry. Here is a huge area of

virgin forests which await development. The same applies to the special needs of the forest industry in Newfoundland, where the forests are beginning to be infected by the woolly aphis insect. This scourge of the forests could very well have dire economic consequences on the woods industry in Newfoundland, and the possibility of the constructing of roads through the forests so as to fight this pest is one which could be considered by the development board.
The fisheries of the whole Atlantic coast certainly need attention, not so much because the fisheries are dwindling as the fact that our competitor nations have advanced much further than we have in the production of fish and have given us the kind of competition in historic markets which has been making it extremely difficult for the fishing industry to survive. That certainly applies to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. Some of the problems of the fisheries are such that they can be met with the expenditure of modest sums of money. A board such as the Atlantic development board would naturally look into the possibility of direct financial assistance to fishermen who wish to improve their fishing equipment. They would consider, I would hope, the position of men who used to be fishermen, who have worked at other vocations for a number of years, whose fishing gear is not operable any more and who would consider being re-established in the fishing industry.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
Clause 1 stands.
Progress reported.
